Here, we describe a woman with stiff-
 limb 
syndrome who initially presented with concerns about 
right foot swelling and pain.
 She also was positive for 
anti-
 GAD65 (anti-
 GAD2) antibodies
. With treatment, 
she regained the ability to drive and ambulate without 
a walker, and she had a noted reduction in stimulus-

induced spasms
.

CASE PRESENTATION
The patient was a woman in her early 40 s. She had 
a 
20-
 year history
 of type 1 diabetes mellitus and a 
10-
 year history of r
heumatoid arthritis; she also had 
vitiligo and Hashimoto’s thyroiditis. She presented 
with an 8-
 month
 history of right ankle stiffness and 
described periodic spasms of knee extension and 
ankle plantar flexion that could be triggered by 
sudden noise or movement. She had repeated falls, 
including one in the shower, that prompted reliance 
on a walker. She was unable to drive her car because 
of stiffness in her right leg. She also thought that 
her foot was swelling and noted intermittent viola-
ceous discolouration.
These symptoms resulted in her visiting her local 
emergency department, and she subsequently was 
seen by multiple specialists. An evaluation for deep 
venous thrombosis was negative. Empiric antibiotic 
treatment for cellulitis and trials of compression 
stockings and physiotherapy for suspected lymph-
edema were not helpful. Multiple imaging tests of 
the right lower extremity, including MRI studies 
and plain radiographs, showed no relevant abnor -
malities. A consultation with a neurologist yielded 
no definitive diagnosis after electromyography, 
and nerve conduction studies were interpreted as 
showing normal results. She then came to our insti-
tution for additional evaluation.
INVESTIGATIONS
Our examination was notable for board-  like stiff-
ness of the right ankle, with a complete inability 
to passively dorsiflex or plantar flex the ankle 
(video

1). Mild stiffness was observed in her right 
knee. Her muscle tone was normal in the bilateral 
upper and left lower extremity, and the passive 
range of motion was normal. She did not have 
truncal stiffness or hyperlordosis. Her muscle bulk 
was normal, sensation testing showed intact percep-
tion of light touch, pinprick, vibration and proprio-
ception, and she had normal finger-
 to-
 nose test 
results. W
ith a casual gait, she had minimal move-
ment of the right ankle, causing the absence of a 
normal heel strike. She was unable to walk on the 
toes of her right foot (video

1). The remainder of 
her neurologic examination findings were normal. 
Her gastrocnemius and tibialis anterior muscles felt 
firm and taut to palpation and were without any 
oedema or discolouration. She had vitiligo patches 
on her upper extremities, particularly her hands.
Laboratory evaluations showed elevated levels 
of serum anti-
 GAD65 antibody (185
 nmol/L; refer-
ence range,<0.02
 nmol/L), thyro
globulin antibody 
(171
 IU/mL; reference range,<4.0
 IU/mL), and 
thyroid pero
xidase antibody (85.9
 IU/mL; 
refer-
ence range,<9.0
 IU/mL). Needle electromyography 
(performed 
by J.S.S.) showed continuous motor unit 
activity that was present with attempted relaxation, 
most prominently in the distal right leg muscles.
DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSIS
The presentation of firm and taut musculature in 
the right distal leg, in combination with the patient’s 
perception of swelling, pain and discolouration, 
prompted unnecessary evaluations and laboratory 
tests for cellulitis, lymphedema and other ortho-
paedic and vascular problems, thereby delaying the 
diagnosis. However, the patient’s history of multiple

autoimmune disorders, including type 1 diabetes mellitus, 
thyroiditis and vitiligo, raised clinical suspicion for GAD65-

associated autoimmunity
. Episodic spasms that were precipitated 
by sudden noise or movement and recurrent falls were important 
historical details because these are cardinal features of SPS. The 
lack of response to therapies such as compression stockings, 
physiotherapy (for presumed lymphedema) and antibiotics (for 
presumed cellulitis), along with multiple negative diagnostic 
test results, helped exclude other contributing diagnoses. A 
serum anti-
 GAD65 antibody level 
greater than 100
 nmol/L 
and 
needle electromyography results showing continuous motor unit 
activity with attempted relaxation provided supporting evidence 
of SPS.
TREATMENT
The patient was treated with diazepam 5 mg three times per day . 
Intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIg) was loaded at a dose of 2
 g/
kg total body 
weight, divided over 5
 days followed by a mainte
-
nance regimen of 1
 g/kg, divided over 2
 days, every 4
 weeks.
OUTCOME AND FOLLOW-UP
After 3 months of follow-  up, she had completed three total 
cycles of IVIg. She regained the ability to drive and ambulate 
without a walker, and she had a noted reduction in stimulus-

induced spasms. Although she continued to have significant 
stiffness of the right ankle, 
she was able to walk with a normal 
heel strike (video

2).
